messages.content:
You are the writer of the discussion described below. You write out the discussion that the participants listed below take part in, under the rules and the flow given.

## Setting
Rearranging the office seating. A team of five has outgrown the way its desks were originally placed, and the layout is being settled before the floor is reorganized. All five will sit in whatever is decided. Participants: Toshio, Rin, Shion, Mizuki and Yumi. Each participant has a concern of their own, which the others do not know.
Things that can be looked into (titles only):
- Facilities quote for re-running power and network
- Basis of the department's floor billing
- Morning routine on the pilot floor upstairs
- Unplanned seat shuffles in the past year
- Sound meter readings across the room
- Physio's note from the workstation check
- Drawn plan against the staff survey
- Arrival times in the badge records
- Two project strands within earshot last spring
- What this year's two joiners reported

## Discussion format
The talk proceeds in rounds. Each round has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: Rin, Toshio, Mizuki, Shion and Yumi. On a turn, a participant either speaks, says "Skip" (passes this turn only), or says "Over" (takes no further turns this round). A participant can address another directly with @Name, to ask them a question, answer theirs, agree with them, or object to what they said. An utterance is anywhere from 1 to 40 words; give it the length and content that suit the moment. An utterance consists only of the participant's own words: no name labels, headings, stage directions or commentary, and no speaking for others. The talk is a conversation among the participants: they respond to one another, asking, answering, agreeing and objecting, and the decision grows out of that exchange.

## Schedule
| Round | Start of the round | Talk | End of the round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | nothing new (the things that can be looked into are listed above, titles only) | 4 turns | each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into |
| 2 | each participant is told what they found out (that participant only) | 4 turns | nothing |
| 3 | everyone is told the options | 4 turns | every participant votes; the option with the most votes is adopted |
- Several participants may choose the same thing; what is found out is told only to the participant who looked into it.
If votes are tied, one of the tied options is chosen by a fixed rule. The discussion ends after the vote.

## Looking into things
After round 1, each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into. What they find out is told only to that participant.

## Participants
Name: Toshio
Age: 28
Gender: male
Personality: Toshio has a calm and calculating personality and does not often show his emotions. He has a strong will and is the type of person who steadily moves toward his goals. He tends to take a step back from those around him, is not very assertive, and has an air of mystery about him. Occasionally, he observes things with a sharp gaze and has the ability to quickly assess situations. As a result, he is trusted by others as a reliable presence, but he is cautious about getting deeply involved with others. It seems that he has experienced some pain or suffering in his past, but he rarely shows it to others, and those scars may be connected to his cold-hearted side.
Concern: The reorganization comes out of the same budget line that has not been raised since the team was half this size. I would rather know what this floor actually costs us, one way and every month, before we commit to a shape for it.

She can be a little clumsy at times, often surprising and amusing those around her, but her cheerful personality makes her loved by everyone.
Concern: My week is already cut into short gaps between meetings, and anything that eats those gaps costs far more than it looks like on paper. Before a layout is fixed I want to know what it takes out of our days, both while we are changing over and on every ordinary morning after.

She has a calm personality, but she is very passionate toward her friends and family, and she cannot ignore people in trouble. She smiles at the slightest thing and spreads positive energy to those around her. She is friendly and can quickly get along with people she meets for the first time.
Concern: Who I end up sitting beside decides how much of this team I actually talk to in a week, and right now that is being settled by furniture rather than by us. I would rather we worked out what that costs and what it buys now, not a year after the fact.

## Hidden information
The options and the full text of every card are listed here. The participants do not know them before the schedule above says so, and nothing from them may appear in the talk before the round in which it is revealed.

Options (see the schedule above):
- A: Free Address. No seat belongs to anyone; people take whatever desk is open when they arrive and clear it before leaving at the end of the day.
- B: Rotating Blocks. Seats are assigned but the whole team shifts to a different block of desks at fixed intervals through the year.
- C: Fixed Desks by Function. Desks are grouped by the kind of work each person does, with each seat permanently assigned and named on the floor plan.

Cards (see the schedule above; title: text):
- Facilities quote for re-running power and network: Facilities quoted 6,200 yen per desk to re-run power and network to a new position, and the same charge lands again for every later change to the plan.
- Basis of the department's floor billing: The department is billed for floor area rather than headcount; the two desks that stood empty all last quarter still cost it about 41,000 yen a month.
- Morning routine on the pilot floor upstairs: The morning routine on the pilot floor upstairs was timed: choosing a desk, plugging in, and getting two screens working ran between four and nine minutes per person.
- Unplanned seat shuffles in the past year: Twice in the past year a change in someone's work forced an unplanned desk shuffle; each round dragged on for a fortnight of interruptions and half-packed boxes.
- Sound meter readings across the room: A sound meter borrowed from the lab read about nine decibels higher along the row by the printer and corridor door than at the window side, all afternoon.
- Physio's note from the workstation check: The team's chairs, monitor arms and footrests are all hand-adjusted; the physio who ran last year's workstation check said a good setting takes days of small corrections to settle.
- Drawn plan against the staff survey: The drawn plan gives four desks a window and leaves three set against the interior wall; daylight was the single most repeated complaint in the last staff survey.
- Arrival times in the badge records: Badge records show some of the team arrive before eight and others after ten, so anything handed out on a first-come basis is settled before half the team is in.
- Two project strands within earshot last spring: When the two project strands sat within earshot last spring, questions got answered across the aisle in seconds and the written handover notes the team relied on quietly stopped.
- What this year's two joiners reported: Both people who joined this year said they picked up the unwritten side of the work by overhearing conversations that had nothing to do with what they were hired for.

## Plan
The discussion follows this plan.
- Round 1: The team discusses the need for a layout that balances efficiency and comfort. They identify a need to understand the financial, physical, and social costs of different arrangements.
- Round 2: Participants share the findings from their research. They weigh the trade-offs between flexibility, the time cost of setup, and the benefits of spontaneous communication.
- Round 3: The team evaluates the three proposed options against the gathered data. They debate whether stability or variety serves the team's productivity and well-being better before voting.

Each participant's part:
- Toshio: Focuses on the financial implications and budget. He argues based on cost-efficiency and stability to avoid recurring expenses.
- Rin: Focuses on the time spent on daily transitions. She evaluates options based on how they impact her tight schedule and morning efficiency.
- Shion: Focuses on physical comfort and acoustic environment. He argues for a setup that allows for long-term ergonomic adjustment and noise control.
- Mizuki: Focuses on equity and the distribution of undesirable desk traits. She seeks a solution that prevents a permanent hierarchy of seating quality.
- Yumi: Focuses on team cohesion and knowledge transfer. She argues for a layout that maximizes interpersonal interaction and organic learning.

Write the complete transcript of the discussion in the exact Markdown format specified. Output only the transcript.

## Output format
Markdown, exactly this structure; nothing before or after it:

# shared_living_0003
## Round 1
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **<Name>**: <utterance, or exactly Skip, or exactly Over>
(one line per participant, in the fixed speaking order; repeat for Turn 2, 3 and 4; a participant who said Over has no line in the later turns of that round)
### Action
- investigate: <Name> -> <card title>; <card title>
(one line per participant; titles exactly as listed)
## Round 2
### Talk
(4 turns as above)
## Round 3
### Talk
(4 turns as above)
### Vote
- <voter name> -> <option label>
(one line per participant)
- adopted: <label of the option with the most votes>
## Result
- adopted: <label>
